title: Elon Musk says Tesla must refund Cybertruck deposits to ‘a lot of people’; he touted 250K reservations back in 2019
detail:
Elon Musk says Tesla must refund Cybertruck deposits to ‘a lot of people’; he touted 250K reservations back in 2019
Becky Robertson
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 5:15 PM CST 4 min read
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Following Tesla's announcement that it will cease production of its famed Cybertruck just three and a half years after the space-age model made its disruptive debut, the EV titan is preparing to process refunds to customers who had put down deposits for a 2027 delivery. And apparently, there are "a lot."

CEO Elon Musk wrote in an X post on Sunday that demand for the stainless-steel pickups is now outpacing the rate at which Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) can make them at its factory and global headquarters in Austin, which is the only hub that manufactures the vehicle.

"We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people," he wrote in the post, which came two days after he broke the hearts of Cybertruck fans with the initial news of its end to make way for fabrication of the flashy new autonomous Cybercab.

How much were the deposits and how much will Tesla have to pay out?

The brand's website currently states that reservation "pre-order payments" are fully refundable up until the car's shipping date.

But there has been some confusion between the initial reservation fee and the order fee that a client pays once they reach the front of the reservation waitlist and are able to customize their vehicle.

Reservations opened up when the truck was first unveiled in 2019 for a mere $100 USD, a tiny fraction of the $60,990 to $120,000 price tag of the angular, head-turning set of wheels.

This price was briefly bumped to $250 when the first of them began hitting the roads at the end of 2023. Then in August 2024, the reservation system was done away with entirely, and direct orders were opened up to the general public without any waiting period. The fee to configure and lock in a Cybertruck, the order fee, was also set at $250, and was non-refundable at the time.

Of course, now that Tesla is the one cancelling orders, these funds will be returned to would-be Cybertruck owners.

According to the latest sales figures via Bloomberg, a total of 7,133 of the machines were purchased in the U.S. during the first five months of this year, compared to the 250,000 Musk touted in 2019. But, the model's discontinuation has prompted a reported surge in interest.

Securitize to Acquire River One, Expanding Into $6 Trillion Asset-Backed Finance Market

Tokenization platform Securitize (NYSE: $SECZ) agreed Monday to acquire River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform built around the stablecoin economy, as it expands into a private asset-backed finance market estimated at more than $6 trillion.

The acquisition, announced alongside Securitize's third-quarter financial results, would expand its tokenization infrastructure into warehouse financing, allowing institutions to borrow against pools of loans and other assets before selling, refinancing or otherwise distributing them. The deal also represents the first major deployment of the roughly $400 million CEO Carlos Domingo told said in July the company planned to allocate toward acquisitions following its public listing.

According to Securitize's earnings announcement, River One was incubated by Framework Ventures and backed by Framework and Maple Finance. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Domingo described credit as "one of the most exciting emerging asset classes" for blockchain-based financial markets. The private asset-backed finance market was valued at approximately $6.1 trillion in 2024 and is projected to exceed $9 trillion by 2029, according to a KKR report cited by CoinDesk.

Securitize also reported third-quarter revenue of $18.6 million, up 13% from $16.5 million a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Tokenization revenue climbed 28% to $11.5 million, while asset servicing revenue declined 6% to $7.2 million. Average tokenized assets on the platform reached a record $5.0 billion, an increase of 39%, with $4.8 billion in assets on the platform as of Sept. 30. Transaction volume increased 20% to $4.3 billion. Meanwhile, assets under administration in its fund services business fell 29% to $25.2 billion.

The company reported a net loss of $66.3 million, or $0.41 per diluted share, compared with net income of $4.1 million in the same quarter last year. Approximately $60 million, or roughly 90% of the reported loss, stemmed from largely non-cash expenses and accounting charges associated with its business combination and public listing. These included a $23.2 million change in the fair value of earnout liabilities and a $20.6 million loss related to the settlement of convertible instruments.

The Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) surged 2.74% to 25,253 as semiconductors rallied, while the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) rose 2.35% to 7,550 as it clawed back losses from its worst weekly performance since April 2025. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) gained 2.15% to 52,390 as it recovered levels lost after the U.S. midterm elections.

Gold prices rose 1.74% to $4,138.25 as of U.S. market close, and the 10-Year Treasury yield edged 0.02% higher to 4.88%. All sectors finished in the green, with industrial stocks -- up 4.59% -- leading the gainers. Basic materials and consumer cyclical stocks also had a solid day.

Today's biggest moves

Nvidia shares fell over 4% after the company launched an internal probe into its CEO's personal relationships. Cloudflare closed up almost 10% as investors favored broader AI infrastructure. Tesla rose over 5%, as its robo-taxis expanded into more cities.

What this means for investors

Stocks rebounded today, erasing some of last week's losses as dip buying and falling oil prices boosted sentiment. Even the difficulties at tech heavyweight Nvidia did not derail the wider semiconductor gains. Investors are monitoring leadership and security risks at the firm, as well as watching to see how the firm's difficulties will impact the AI sector.

Shares of Constellation Energy gained over 10% after it beat earnings estimates and upped its full-year guidance. AI-infrastructure stocks tumbled last week on concerns that the Democrats' success in the midterms might slow the data center build-out. Today's results boosted the sector, including NRG Energy and GE Vernova.

For investors, this market resilience is reassuring. However, last week's sell-off and the Nvidia revelations are a reminder to be mindful of the risk level in your portfolio, particularly your exposure to AI-related stocks.

Lee Samaha, The Motley Fool

Cathie Wood's Ark Invest clearly believes that Tesla's (NASDAQ: TSLA) robotaxi business will be a huge success. In fact, its base case for Tesla stock in 2031 calls for robotaxi to account for 81% of its expected $4,400 value. Moreover, Ark Invest argues that Tesla's cash flows from its robotaxi network could be used to support Space Exploration Technologies' (NASDAQ: SPCX) capital expenditures in the event of a merger. Is it time to buy Tesla stock?

Robotaxi cash flow and SpaceX spending

If you believe that robotaxi will be successful and, more importantly, that its dedicated robotaxi, Cybercab, will have a long-term competitive cost advantage, then the answer is no. The secure stream of recurring revenue from robotaxi is better left with Tesla rather than funding SpaceX's growth ambitions. In other words, if robotaxi is successful, then the stock will appreciate significantly anyway.

Furthermore, there are five reasons why Tesla shouldn't be part of SpaceX.

Image source: Tesla.
Why a SpaceX and Tesla merger might not be great for Tesla shareholders

First, SpaceX is a fine company, but you have to be fully on board with its growth prospects and valuation to, de facto, turn yourself into an investor in its growth by giving up your share of cash flow from robotaxi as a Tesla shareholder in place of funding SpaceX capital spending.

Second, given the uncertainty around the robotaxi rollout, if you are confident in its success and it occurs, the stock will appreciate, and Tesla shareholders can negotiate a better price for any takeover.

Third, as previously discussed regarding a merger between SpaceX and Tesla, the reality is that these two companies have significantly different risk and capital profiles. Yes, Tesla's investments in robotaxi and Optimus robots require significant up-front capital, but Tesla has the resources to fund them and is set to ramp up its robotaxi rollout in 2027. In other words, it's about to start migrating toward becoming a highly cash-generative company with a stream of reliable income. This contrasts with SpaceX's need to fund artificial intelligence infrastructure and launch services, while bearing the ongoing risk of a launch failure. Simply put, these companies have significantly different risk and capital profiles.

title: Musk says many Cybertruck buyers will get deposits back as production ends, arguing ‘opportunity cost’ is vastly outweighed by new robotaxi
detail:
Musk says many Cybertruck buyers will get deposits back as production ends, arguing ‘opportunity cost’ is vastly outweighed by new robotaxi
Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 2:30 PM CST 4 min read
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

After sidelining the Cybertruck as he bets Tesla's future on the autonomous Cybercab, Elon Musk now says customers still waiting for their electric truck may not get one after all. 

In an early Monday post on X, he said the number of Cybertrucks ordered "far exceeds our production rate," which means many buyers will be out of luck following the CEO's announcement Friday that Tesla would be "winding down" the electric truck's production by the middle of next year.

"We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people," Musk said Monday.

The news comes as some fans of the boxy and futuristic-looking Cybertruck said on social media that they were putting in new orders or upgrading their existing Cybertruck orders before the vehicle ends production. As of Monday, Tesla's website seemed to still be accepting new orders.

Musk said in his latest post that Tesla was shutting down Cybertruck production not because the vehicle was unprofitable but because, "the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production."

The Cybertruck, unlike other Tesla vehicles like Model Y, has struggled to reach and maintain high sales since it was released in 2023. When the vehicle was first announced in 2019, Musk hailed it as Tesla's best product "ever." He later predicted Tesla would make between 250,000 and half-a-million units of the vehicle per year. Yet, between 2024 and 2025, Cybertruck sales plummeted 48% to 20,237 from 38,965.

Through the third quarter of this year, Tesla had sold an estimated 11,586, according to Kelley Blue Book. Meanwhile, Tesla sold 262,491 Model Ys and 106,962 Model 3s over that same time.

In recent years, Tesla has discontinued other models like the Model S luxury sedan and Model X SUV, narrowing its consumer vehicle lineup as Musk increasingly shifts the company's focus to autonomous vehicles, but also humanoid robots. Tesla's focus could drift further away from cars as it explores a merger with Musk's other public company, SpaceXAI.

A cult following

To be sure, the Cybertruck has still amassed a cult following for its unique design despite, or sometimes because of, the association with Musk, whose rightward shift once made him a close adviser of President Trump and the leader of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). 

After a brief falling out with Trump, he returned to the fold and reportedly spent as much as $474 million in the midterm election cycle to boost Republican candidates. But many of his preferred candidates lost, following a surprisingly strong showing for the Democratic Party in the midterms last week.
